content: Many individuals infected with the Zika virus do not exhibit symptoms or may only experience mild symptoms. However, Zika virus infection during pregnancy can result in severe birth defects. The virus is present at low levels in many regions globally, but outbreaks can occur. Since there is no vaccine or specific treatment for Zika, travelers should take measures to prevent infection during travel and avoid spreading the virus upon returning home. For information on countries and territories with Zika, refer to the Zika Travel Information page. How is Zika virus spread? 1. Mosquito bites: Zika virus is primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected mosquito. Mosquitoes become infected when they bite a person already carrying the virus. These infected mosquitoes can then transmit the virus to other individuals through subsequent bites. 2. Mother-to-child transmission: A pregnant woman infected with Zika can pass the virus to her developing fetus during pregnancy or at the time of birth. 3. Sexual transmission: Zika can be transmitted through sexual contact with an infected individual. The virus can be present in semen for an extended period, lasting months after infection, and can be transmitted during this time. It is important to note that even asymptomatic individuals can spread the virus. What can travelers do to prevent Zika? Pregnant women should not travel to areas experiencing Zika outbreaks (marked as red zones on the Zika Travel Information map) due to the risk of severe birth defects associated with Zika infection during pregnancy. Before traveling to areas with a potential risk of Zika (marked as purple zones on the map), pregnant women and couples planning pregnancy within the next three months should consult their healthcare provider. They should carefully evaluate the risks and potential consequences of traveling to these regions, as the level of risk may not be accurately known, and new outbreaks may not be promptly detected or reported. All travelers to areas with Zika risk should: 1. Take measures to prevent mosquito bites, such as using insect repellents, wearing protective clothing, and staying in accommodations with proper mosquito control. 2. Use condoms consistently or abstain from sexual activity to prevent Zika transmission during travel. These precautions should continue after returning home to prevent spreading the virus to others. Special precautions for specific groups The CDC recommends additional precautions for: 1. Pregnant women: Avoid traveling to areas with Zika outbreaks (red zones on the map). If considering travel to areas with potential Zika risk (purple zones), discuss travel plans with a healthcare provider and carefully weigh the risks. Consider factors such as the destination, reasons for travel, feelings about potential risks, and ability to prevent mosquito bites during travel and for three weeks after returning. Follow strict measures to prevent sexual transmission of Zika during the trip. After returning, attend routine prenatal care appointments and inform your healthcare provider about any travel history and potential Zika exposure. Report any symptoms of Zika infection promptly. If your partner travels to areas with Zika risk (red or purple zones), use condoms consistently during sex or abstain from sexual activity for the remainder of the pregnancy, even if your partner does not exhibit symptoms or feel unwell. 2. Partners of pregnant women: If traveling to areas with Zika risk, use condoms consistently during sex or abstain from sexual activity for the duration of the pregnancy to prevent transmission to the pregnant partner. By adhering to these guidelines, individuals can reduce the risk of Zika virus infection and its associated complications.
